strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-motivated bottleneck (manual spectral vetting in astronomy) with an end-to-end tool-augmented VLM agent; the iMCoT design explicitly mirrors the documented expert inspection workflow, which is a sensible and clearly articulated design principle.

Comprehensive evaluation: in-distribution results on SpecVI-Bench, zero-shot cross-survey generalization (LAMOST→SDSS/DESI), zero-shot cross-task transfer (O/B/A types), ablations over SFT/RL/tool access (Table 4), and training dynamics in Appendix F. The ablation cleanly shows both stages are necessary and that interactive re-rendering (not just global views) is essential.

Large, well-supported empirical gains: macro-F1 from 28.3 (base) to 76.5 (7B), beating proprietary o3 (52.3) and fine-tuned specialist models (64.9), with cross-survey degradation of only a few points versus 13-20 points for specialist models.

A new benchmark (SpecVI-Bench) with hard negatives constructed via rejection sampling to approximate the high-confusion vetting regime, deliberate test imbalance, and explicit steps to prevent contamination between cold-start trajectories and the test split. Statistics and prompts are documented in the appendices.

Human reliability evaluation with six credentialed astronomers (PhD + spectroscopy publications), a defined 0-5 rubric, comparison of human and LLM-judge score distributions, Spearman correlations across four judges, and a pairwise preference study versus o3.
Reproducibility support: code/data/models promised at a project page, released prompt templates (Table 6), rollout algorithm (Algorithm 1), dataset statistics (Table 5), and hardware/training setup.
The limitations section is candid and specific (limited object types, dependence on expert cold-start trajectories, no calibration/abstraction mechanisms).
weaknesses: Label validity of the benchmark's hard negatives is not fully established: negatives are 'spectra not listed in official catalogs with weak-classifier probability > 0.8'. Some of these could be genuine undiscovered rare objects or contaminants mislabeled as negatives, which could systematically bias F1 for all methods. The paper does not report any expert verification of a sample of these negatives.

Human evaluation lacks inter-annotator agreement statistics (e.g., Krippendorff's alpha) among the six experts; only human-vs-LLM-judge correlations are reported, making rater consistency claims ('substantial rater consistency') under-supported.

A substantial part of the discriminative knowledge (key indicators, contaminant patterns) is supplied via expert-written prompts (Table 6) and GPT-5-generated trajectories; while baselines receive the same prompt, the paper does not isolate how much performance derives from the prompt/instruction content versus the learned inspection policy. An ablation on prompt detail would strengthen the claims.

Some evidence of imperfect reasoning quality: the Figure 2 example trace states velocities of 'tens to hundreds of km/s' in a context where FWHM > 1000 km/s is the diagnostic, a physically inconsistent statement that slightly undercuts the 'physically consistent' claim, even if it is only an illustration.

Cross-survey test sets are small (~50 positives, ~250 negatives per task) and restricted to three of five task types, so generalization estimates carry nontrivial variance; no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported for any comparison.

Fit to ACL is moderate: the core contributions are domain-science application of existing techniques (GRPO, cold-start SFT, tool-augmented zooming similar to DeepEyes/Chain-of-Focus/Mini-o3). The methodological novelty relative to that line of work is incremental—mainly the domain tool, trajectory curation pipeline, and benchmark.

Minor presentation issues: abstract has a grammatical error ('Due to the limited... The final vetting'), inconsistent capitalization ('like Astronomers'), and some hyperparameter detail for training is deferred/thin.
WD performance remains weak (F1 53.6, below CarbonNet/AstroCLIP on that task), which is acknowledged only implicitly; per-task failure analysis is absent.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-motivated bottleneck (expert visual vetting of rare-object candidates in spectroscopic surveys) with a complete, end-to-end system (tool-augmented iMCoT agent, cold-start SFT, GRPO-based RL) rather than a partial prototype.

Empirical results are strong and extensive: large gains over both proprietary VLMs (o3, GPT-4.1) and fine-tuned specialist deep models on five tasks, plus zero-shot cross-survey (SDSS/DESI) and cross-task (O/B/A types) generalization evaluations that go beyond a single in-distribution table.

Human expert evaluation is unusually thorough for this venue: six PhD-level astronomers, a documented rubric (Table 7), a custom annotation interface, LLM-judge correlation analysis, and pairwise preference comparisons against o3.

Ablations are informative and support the design claims: the two-stage recipe is shown necessary (#0 vs #1/#2 nearly doubles F1), and removing tool access degrades performance substantially (#4), which supports the central 'think-with-spectral-image' thesis.

The benchmark construction (SpecVI-Bench) thoughtfully mirrors the vetting stage via rejection-sampled hard negatives and deliberately imbalanced test splits, and contamination between cold-start trajectories and the test split is explicitly excluded. Code, data, and models are stated to be released, and appendices provide prompts, dataset statistics, and the RL rollout algorithm, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the pipeline (cold-start SFT on curated trajectories + outcome-reward GRPO with loss-masked tool tokens) closely follows existing think-with-image work (DeepEyes, Mini-o3, Chain-of-Focus, Pixel Reasoner). The main contribution is domain transfer plus a domain-specific rendering tool; the paper does not clearly isolate what is scientifically new versus re-applied.

The evaluation may partially measure rule-following rather than visual reasoning: each task prompt embeds detailed expert-written diagnostic criteria (Table 6), so the binary decision space is heavily constrained. No experiment tests whether the zoomed regions are causally responsible for correct decisions (e.g., feeding incorrect/perturbed zoom crops, or ablating tool evidence at inference), leaving the interpretability/trustworthiness claims weakly substantiated.

Potential label noise in SpecVI-Bench is not analyzed: negatives are defined as 'not listed in official catalogs' with classifier probability > 0.8, which conflates true unlisted rare objects with contaminants, and no expert audit of test-split labels is reported. This uncertainty propagates to all headline F1 numbers.

No statistical rigor around the results: single training runs, no seeds, no confidence intervals or significance tests, despite differences that sometimes decide claims (e.g., Spec-o3-3B vs 7B, or margins over GaiaNet's accuracy). The WD task for Spec-o3-7B (F1 53.6) is notably weaker than 3B (43.2→53.6 is actually a gain, but both lag far behind other tasks) and this anomaly is not analyzed.

Human evaluation reports distributions and Spearman correlations but no inter-annotator agreement statistics (e.g., Krippendorff's alpha) for the six raters, and LLM judges scoring their own-family trajectories raises circularity concerns; the sample (100 trajectories) is small relative to the strength of the reliability conclusions.

Fit to the ACL scope is arguable: this is an AI4Science/agent application paper whose core techniques and evaluation conventions are closer to CV/ML venues; the NLP-specific contribution (multimodal CoT trajectory format) is modest.

Writing contains minor but noticeable issues (e.g., capitalization inconsistencies like 'like Astronomers', 'State-of-the-Art' in the abstract, a typo'd sentence opening in the abstract), and some claims ('first tool-augmented VLM-based agent that inspects spectra like Astronomers') are hard to verify and stated without hedging.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly framed problem: automating the manual expert-vetting bottleneck in spectroscopic surveys is a genuine, practical application for tool-augmented multimodal agents, and the 'think-with-spectral-image' analogy to astronomer workflows is a clean, defensible design principle.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: results span in-distribution (SpecVI-Bench), cross-survey (LAMOST→SDSS/DESI), and cross-task (unseen O/B/A types) settings, with baselines from three distinct categories (specialist deep models, proprietary VLMs, open-source VLMs), and consistent large gains (macro-F1 28.3→76.5).

Thorough ablations (Table 4) that separately isolate SFT, RL, and tool access, plus training-dynamics analysis (Appendix F), which substantiate the two-stage post-training claim rather than only asserting it.

Human evaluation with six credentialed astronomers, a defined 0-5 rubric, a custom annotation interface, and cross-validation of judgments against four LLM judges with Spearman correlations — a level of reliability verification rarely seen in agent papers.

A new benchmark (SpecVI-Bench) with a vetting-realistic hard-negative construction procedure and contamination controls between trajectory data and test splits; code, data, and models are stated to be released, supporting reproducibility.

The paper is well organized, with a formalized iMCoT state/action formulation, an explicit reward function, a rollout algorithm, and detailed appendices (prompts, dataset statistics, survey backgrounds).
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is moderate: the recipe (cold-start SFT on curated trajectories + GRPO with outcome rewards + a zoom tool) closely mirrors existing think-with-image systems (DeepEyes, Mini-o3, Chain-of-Focus, Pixel Reasoner). The contribution is a domain transfer plus a new tool, but the paper does not compare against an existing think-with-image framework fine-tuned on the same SpecVI-Bench data, which would more cleanly isolate what is domain-specific versus generic.

Potential label noise in the benchmark: hard negatives are defined as spectra with weak-classifier probability > 0.8 that are absent from official catalogs. Such sources could include genuine rare objects missed by the catalogs, so some 'negative' labels may be wrong; no audit of negative-sample purity (e.g., expert spot-checks) is reported, and this asymmetry could differentially affect models.

No variance reporting: results appear to be single training runs without seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests, despite moderate test-set sizes (e.g., ~210-237 positives per task; ~50 positives in cross-survey settings), where F1 estimates can be noisy.

The reliability study is on only 100 sampled trajectories, and the close human-LLM-judge agreement may partly reflect shared biases (e.g., LLM judges favoring LLM-generated prose); the pairwise preference protocol (who rated, blinding, per-annotator agreement) is underspecified in the main text.

Some results are uneven and under-analyzed: WD F1 is markedly lower (53.6) and Spec-o3-3B accuracy on WD (78.5) is below specialist baselines, yet the paper offers little analysis of why; the claimed workflow 'fidelity' of reasoning is validated via coherence scoring rather than verifying that zoomed regions actually contain the cited diagnostic features.

Writing has minor issues (e.g., abstract 'Due to the limited generalization..., The final vetting', occasional typos), and the OA score should not be inflated by the breadth of the benchmark alone; the core scientific question — whether the agent's decisions rest on correct astrophysical evidence rather than shortcut cues — remains only partially validated.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: the final vetting stage of rare-object cataloging is a genuine, quantified bottleneck (e.g., 323 confirmed CVs from 170k screened candidates), and the paper convincingly frames it as an interactive 'think-with-spectral-image' process rather than a passive classification problem.

Sound two-stage methodology: cold-start SFT on ~1k rigorously audited expert trajectories (GPT-5 drafted, three independent astronomers revised and voted) followed by outcome-based GRPO with token-masked tool outputs is a careful, well-justified design, and the loss masking choice is explicitly motivated.

Comprehensive evaluation suite: in-distribution SpecVI-Bench, cross-survey (SDSS/DESI), cross-task (O/B/A types), and extreme-case (QSO, low-SNR) generalization, plus ablations over training stages, tool access, and SFT data scale. The ablations (e.g., tool removal costs ~20-30 F1; SFT+RL interaction) substantively support the central claims.

Reliability is assessed beyond accuracy: human expert scoring of 100 reasoning trajectories by six PhD-level astronomers, Spearman correlation with four LLM judges, and pairwise preference studies against o3 across three surveys, supporting the interpretability/trust claims.

Strong empirical results with released code/data/models: 76.5 macro-F1 for 7B vs 52.3 for o3 and 28.3 for the base model, with substantial gains retained zero-shot on unseen surveys and tasks; few-shot adaptation (96 synthetic trajectories) nearly closes the QSO gap, demonstrating a scalable bootstrapping recipe.

SpecVI-Bench is a thoughtful contribution in itself: hard negatives via rejection sampling specifically target the vetting stage (high-confusion contaminants), which prior screening-oriented datasets lack, and train/test contamination is explicitly controlled.
weaknesses: Benchmark validity rests on synthetic negatives: test negatives are generated by a weak classifier's high-confidence false positives, so the test distribution inherits that classifier's inductive biases. If the weak classifier systematically misses certain contaminant families, SpecVI-Bench may overstate real-world vetting difficulty (or ease). No human audit of the sampled negatives is reported.

Comparison with specialist DL baselines is only partially meaningful: CarbonNet/GaiaNet/AstroCLIP are screening models fine-tuned on the SpecVI-Bench training split but were not designed for this task; the paper acknowledges this (Appendix F) but the headline 'outperforms specialized deep models' claim should be tempered accordingly.

No statistical rigor around headline numbers: test sets are small (~220 positives per task), yet no confidence intervals, seed variance, or significance tests are reported for the gaps that drive the SOTA claim (e.g., 76.5 vs 74.9 vs 73.6 in cross-task).

The strong reliance on expert-written diagnostic rubrics in the task prompt (Table 6) raises the question of how much of the performance is rubric-following versus learned spectral expertise. The cross-task results partially address this, but an ablation with degraded/absent guidelines is missing.

Potential shortcut concerns are not probed: the model reads rendered plots as images; no experiments verify that decisions are actually grounded in the rendered pixels (e.g., corrupted/shuffled plots at test time) rather than metadata or priors.
The ~50x throughput gain over experts depends on unstated assumptions about expert inspection time and pipeline parallelism; it is plausible but loosely substantiated.
Cold-start data is filtered to SNR>10 and drawn from official catalogs, which themselves contain label noise; the effect of noisy positives in the ~1k trajectories is not analyzed.

strengths: Well-motivated application: automating the manual vetting bottleneck in spectroscopic surveys is a genuine practical problem, and the 'think-with-spectral-image' framing that mirrors expert zoom-and-inspect workflows is a sensible and clearly articulated design.

Comprehensive experimental suite: main benchmark, cross-survey (SDSS/DESI) and cross-task (O/B/A types) zero-shot transfer, extreme-case (QSO, low-SNR) evaluation, two-stage training ablations, tool-access ablation, and cold-start data-efficiency studies collectively provide substantial evidence for the central claims.

Reasoning-quality assessment goes beyond accuracy: expert scoring on a defined 0-5 rubric, LLM-judge correlations with human raters, and pairwise preference comparisons against o3 give some support to interpretability claims.

Reproducibility support is comparatively good: benchmark statistics, prompt examples, rollout algorithm, annotation rubric, and a stated release of code/data/models reduce the barrier to independent verification.
The paper is candid in its Limitations section about narrow task coverage, expert-trajectory dependence, and absence of calibration/abstention mechanisms.
Clear writing and organization; the paradigm-comparison appendix (F) properly contextualizes that specialist DL baselines are screening tools rather than direct vetting competitors.
weaknesses: Benchmark circularity: SpecVI-Bench negatives are generated by a rejection-sampling procedure using classifiers trained by the authors, while Spec-o3 is trained on similarly constructed or related distributions. The hard-negative generation process is only loosely specified (acceptance rate 1.74%), making it hard to rule out that the test distribution favors the proposed agent and that absolute F1 values are inflated relative to real vetting conditions.

The 'expert-driven' cold-start pipeline is substantially GPT-5-generated; trajectories are rewritten/audited by three astronomers, but no inter-annotator agreement statistics, acceptance rates, or per-annotator details are reported for the ~1k-trajectory dataset. The strength of the domain-expertise claim is therefore hard to assess, and the pipeline is only partially reproducible given dependence on a proprietary model.

Limited methodological novelty: the core recipe (cold-start SFT on tool-interleaved traces followed by GRPO with token-masked tool outputs) is a direct application of existing think-with-image and agentic-RL techniques to a new data domain; the technical contribution is the tool and data pipeline rather than a new learning method.

Some claims rest on thin evidence: the ~50x throughput gain assumes a ~10 s per-spectrum expert baseline that is asserted rather than measured; human evaluation uses only 100 scored trajectories and 50 pairwise comparisons per survey with no significance testing; Spearman correlations in Figure 4(b) are reported without confidence intervals.

Comparison with proprietary VLMs (GPT-4.1, o3) is not fully controlled: prompt sensitivity, API-side reasoning budgets, and versioning are not discussed, and the S1-VL-32B-SFT baseline using the authors' cold-start data conflates model scale with data effects in an unexamined way.

Several methodological details needed for independent replication are deferred or vague: the weak classifier used for hard-negative sampling, exact SFT/GRPO hyperparameters, the α penalty value, and how format-constraint rewards interact with tool-call masking.

The reasoning 'coherence and physical consistency' evaluation is performed by the same community likely affiliated with the work (six astronomers, no blinding described), so the trustworthiness claims are at risk of confirmation bias; no adversarial probing of explanations is attempted.
Citations to evidently future-dated venues (e.g., ICLR/NeurIPS 2026, 'Fu et al. 2026a') appear, which undermines bibliographic credibility and makes several related-work claims unverifiable.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly positioned problem: automating the expert visual vetting stage of rare-object cataloging, with a compelling analogy between astronomers' iterative zoom-and-inspect workflow and tool-augmented interleaved multimodal chain-of-thought.

Comprehensive and rigorous experimental design: a purpose-built benchmark (SpecVI-Bench) with carefully constructed high-confusion negatives, deliberate train/test imbalance reflecting real rarity, and explicit exclusion of cold-start spectra from the test split to avoid contamination.
Strong empirical results: state-of-the-art macro-F1 (76.5%) substantially above proprietary VLMs (o3 at 52.3%) and specialist deep models, with large gains over the Qwen2.5-VL base models.

Thorough generalization evaluation across three axes (cross-survey on SDSS/DESI, cross-task on O/B/A types, and extreme cases including QSO and low-SNR), supporting the central claim that the agent learns a transferable inspection methodology rather than task-specific memorization.

Informative ablations isolating the contributions of cold-start SFT, RL, and tool access (Table 4), plus data-efficiency and synthetic-trajectory-bootstrap experiments that directly address the practical annotation bottleneck the paper identifies.

Human evaluation with six credentialed expert astronomers, a documented scoring rubric, and cross-validation of LLM judges against human scores; additionally a pairwise preference study across surveys.

Good reproducibility: code, data, and prompts released; detailed appendix coverage of the tool, dataset statistics, prompts, training dynamics, and algorithms; training configuration (hardware, GRPO rollouts, tool-call limits) reported.
Practical relevance addressed via inference-efficiency analysis (~0.2 s/spectrum), and an honest Limitations section acknowledging coverage, workflow-integration, and risk-control gaps.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the two-stage cold-start SFT + outcome-based GRPO recipe and the zoom-on-need visual tool closely follow existing think-with-image systems (GRIT, Pixel-Reasoner, DeepEyes, Chain-of-Focus); the contribution is primarily a careful adaptation to a new domain rather than a new technique.

Missing the most informative baselines: no open-source agentic think-with-image systems (e.g., DeepEyes, Pixel-Reasoner, GRIT) are trained or evaluated on SpecVI-Bench, so it is unclear how much of the gain comes from the framework versus the domain-specific data pipeline; comparison is restricted to generic VLMs and specialist classifiers.

Potential circularity in the evaluation protocol: negative samples are defined by a weak classifier with predicted probability > 0.8, which may systematically favor models whose decision boundary resembles that classifier; the impact of this choice on reported F1 is not analyzed.

The label pipeline has residual noise concerns: positives inherit labels from official LAMOST catalogs that were themselves partially human-vetted, and the quality/inter-annotator agreement of the ~1k cold-start trajectories (GPT-5 generated, expert-revised) is not quantified beyond acceptance votes.

Reliability evaluation has circularity and scale concerns: LLM judges scoring the authors' own model outputs, only 100 sampled trajectories, no inter-annotator agreement statistics for the six experts, and no confidence intervals or significance tests on any reported results.

Macro-F1 advantage over GaiaNet (76.5 vs 64.9) rests partly on an imbalanced test design whose positives/negatives were constructed by the authors; sensitivity of conclusions to the negative-sampling procedure would strengthen the claim.
The ~50x throughput gain over expert inspection is based on stated assumptions (~10 s/spectrum human time) rather than measured expert timing data.

Scope considerations for the ACL community: the work is a domain application in astronomy; its relevance hinges on the transferability of the iCoT training recipe, which is asserted but not demonstrated outside this domain.
